job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup our legal team wants a complete list of the bill's loopholes, ambiguities, and drafting problems: anything that would let us keep operating if it passes as written, or that we can point to as making it unworkable. Can you go through the bill text below and find every one?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Based solely on the supplied text, these are the principal exploitable gaps and drafting or implementation problems. “Every” issue cannot be guaranteed without legislative history, related statutes, and legal review.

1. **Section 2(1)(A)—per-vessel threshold.** The definition covers recovery of *more than* 10,000 metric tons per year “by a single vessel,” leaving exactly 10,000 tons outside the definition and creating an argument that production can be split among vessels to stay below the threshold. It does not say how to measure a year or aggregate affiliated operators, projects, or vessels.

2. **Section 2(1)(A)—scope of covered minerals and activity.** The text does not define “mineral resources” or specify whether processing, transport, or recovery of minerals other than nodules counts. That leaves room to dispute whether particular materials or stages of an operation meet the definition.

3. **Section 2(1)(B)—Secretary’s discretionary standard.** “Risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable” has no stated criteria, process, or evidentiary standard. The Secretary’s determination could therefore be contested as inconsistent, inadequately supported, or beyond the authority the provision grants.

4. **Section 2(2)—narrow “U.S. person” definition.** The definition includes U.S. citizens and corporations organized under state law, but not expressly partnerships, LLCs, trusts, or foreign-organized subsidiaries. Those entities could argue they are outside the prohibition when operating abroad, subject to other applicable law.

5. **Section 2(3)—covered-vessel threshold.** Only vessels *more than* 5,000 gross tons qualify; vessels at or below that threshold are excluded. “Equipped for the recovery” is also undefined, inviting disputes over vessel size, equipment, and whether a vessel is covered.

6. **Sections 2(3) and 4—registry does not track the prohibition.** The registry applies only to covered vessels, while section 3 applies to commercial mining without regard to vessel size. Operators using smaller or differently characterized vessels may avoid registration and reporting even if their activity is prohibited.

7. **Section 3(a)—“person in the United States” is unclear.** The bill does not define when a person is “in” the United States or whether the phrase reaches conduct partly performed here, such as financing or contracting for foreign operations. That creates uncertainty about the prohibition’s territorial reach.

8. **Section 3(a)—“engage in” is undefined.** The bill does not specify whether the prohibition reaches only direct recovery or also financing, equipment supply, contracting, transport, or other support. Both enforcement and potential defendants could dispute which activities count as engaging in mining.

9. **Sections 2(1) and 3(a)—threshold-based avoidance.** Because the prohibition applies only to activity meeting the defined term “commercial deep seabed mining,” low-volume or intermittent recovery may fall outside it unless the Secretary makes a paragraph (B) determination. The bill does not explain how separate operations or successive years are treated.

10. **Section 3(b)—broad existing-operations exception.** The exception covers “mining conducted under an exploration license issued before” enactment, without limiting the amount, duration, location, or type of mining. It does not say whether the license must expressly authorize commercial extraction, or how transfers, renewals, or amendments are treated.

11. **Section 3(c)—environmental-assessment exception.** “For the purpose of environmental assessment” is undefined and has no limits on scale, duration, or incidental recovery. An operator could argue that otherwise prohibited extraction qualifies if conducted as part of an assessment.

12. **Section 4(a)—no registration deadline or registration rules.** The bill does not specify when registration is due or what information NOAA must require, nor does it establish review, denial, or updating procedures. That leaves compliance timing and the registry’s practical utility uncertain.

13. **Section 4(b)—incomplete reporting requirements.** Reports need only “describ[e] the recovery activities” and are not subject to specified content, verification, public-disclosure, or record-retention standards. Operators could submit minimal descriptions, and NOAA has no express authority here to require more detail.

14. **Section 4—no express penalty for registry violations.** Sections 5(a) and (b) penalize violations of section 3, not failures to register or report under section 4. The bill provides no direct penalty for those omissions.

15. **Section 5(a)—penalty date conflicts with effective date.** The civil penalty applies to violations “on or after” enactment, but section 8 delays the Act’s effective date by 180 days. The text does not reconcile whether penalties can attach before the prohibition takes effect.

16. **Section 5(a)—penalty calculation is underspecified.** “Not more than $1,000,000 for each day” does not identify the responsible authority, factors for setting the amount, or how a continuing or multi-actor violation is counted. Those omissions could complicate enforcement and invite challenges to the amount imposed.

17. **Section 5(b)—criminal liability is not further defined.** The bill does not specify what must be willful—conduct, knowledge of the prohibition, or knowledge that the activity meets the statutory definition. That leaves a significant question for prosecutors, defendants, and courts.

18. **Section 6—international agreement is aspirational.** The Secretary need only “seek to negotiate” an agreement; the bill does not require a completed agreement, provide consequences if negotiations fail, or set an implementation mechanism. The 18-month deadline applies to seeking negotiations, not achieving an outcome.

19. **Section 7(a)—termination standard and process are uncertain.** “Without serious harm” is undefined, and the bill sets no deadline or process for the National Academies report or congressional consideration. The joint-resolution condition also leaves unclear what happens if no report or resolution occurs.

20. **Sections 7(a) and 7(b)—duration provisions conflict.** Section 7(a) keeps the prohibition in effect until Congress acts on a report, while section 7(b) says the Act ceases to have effect after ten years. The text does not clarify whether the prohibition automatically ends at ten years regardless of Congress’s findings.

21. **Sections 7(b) and 8—effective ban may be shorter than ten years.** The ten-year sunset runs from enactment, but the Act takes effect only after 180 days. If the sunset controls, the operative period is about six months shorter than ten years.

22. **Sections 3(b), 7(b), and 8—transition rules are missing.** The bill does not say how the grandfathering exception or pending operations are treated during the 180-day delay, or what happens to licenses, penalties, and enforcement at sunset. The interaction of these provisions could generate disputes over both the start and end of coverage.
